title: The ways
hookLine: the schools, the paths, the scholars
tomorrow: Zayd's recital is tonight. which hadith does he open with?

cards: An open house at a mosque in Houston. A visitor stands at the back and watches the rows pray: shoulder to shoulder, same direction, same words. Then she notices something.
The man on the left folds his hands on his chest. The man beside him lets his arms hang straight down at his sides. Afterward she whispers to her friend: so which one of them is doing it right?

teach.b: Under her question is a bigger one: if Muslims do it differently, is it still one faith? The tradition's answer lives in the word madhhab, a way, a school of law.
Among Sunni Muslims, the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools; among Shia Muslims, the Ja'fari school.
Each grew from scholars reading the same Qur'an and the same reports of the Prophet ﷺ, and sometimes landing in different places on details.
Arms at the sides is a common way to pray in the Maliki school and among Shia Muslims; folded hands, in the others. Same qibla. Same Fatiha.
Tradition tells a story worth repeating tonight: a caliph wanted to make Imam Malik's book, the Muwatta, the law in every city.

teach.h: MALIK SAYS NO TO ONE LAW.
teach.b: Malik said no. The companions had scattered to many cities, he said, and each place had learned from them. Now a neighbor, in their own words.
In the Talmud, two schools of rabbis, the houses of Hillel and Shammai, argued for years.
Then, the Talmud says, a voice from heaven declared: these and these are the words of the living God.
Both. And the honest difference: in that same passage the law follows Hillel, because, the Talmud says, his students were gentle and humble and taught Shammai's view before their own.
Among the Muslim schools, no single winner is named; each school's rulings stand side by side.

how: Most Muslims follow, or are shaped by, a school of law (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali among Sunnis, Ja'fari among Shia), and Muslims of different schools pray side by side in the same mosque, facing the same qibla.

the schools and paths within one faith

games.q: who said it — tap the pairs.
p: a way, a school of law
said no to one law for every city
these and these are words of the living God

s: Muslims pray in exactly the same posture everywhere
the schools differ on details, like where the hands rest; the qibla and the Fatiha are shared.
in the Talmud, both Hillel's and Shammai's views are called words of the living God
tradition says Malik refused to make his book the law of every city
the companions had spread to many cities, and each had learned from them.

games.q: at a campus prayer, the person leading follows a different school from yours, and a small detail of how he prays is different. what fits today?
o: pray behind him; the schools are different ways of one prayer.
pray alone afterward, since every detail has to match yours.
pray with him, then correct him privately on the detail.
games.why: the schools read the same sources and land differently on details. same qibla, same Fatiha: Muslims of different schools pray in the same rows.

practice: Bring to mind one teacher on your path, from any school or none: a parent, a weekend-school teacher, an imam, the author of a book that helped. Write them a short thank-you now, a text or a note, naming one thing they taught you.
If they've passed on, say it to them quietly instead.

wordCard.voice: The ways: the schools, the paths, the scholars. Different on details, facing one direction.

orig.note: Arabic: a way one goes; a school of Islamic law.

carryVoice: Something to keep: many ways, one qibla, and an argument kept with kindness. Eight of fifteen.
